newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Africa faces democracy challenge at OAU summit.
newsitem.headline: Africa faces democracy challenge at OAU summit.

text.p: The Organisation of African Unity begins a three-day summit in Zimbabwe on Monday facing one of the biggest issues confronting the continent -- securing democracy.
But its secretary-general says the meeting aims to focus on economic development, and some diplomats fear it may duck the tough political challenges facing the continent.

The summit has been overshadowed by a military coup in the West African state of Sierra Leone, and by events in former Zaire where Laurent Kabila fought his way to power in early May after a seven-month guerrilla campaign against Mobutu Sese Seko, one of the world's longest serving presidents.

OAU officials say Sierra Leone's case demonstrates the need to respect democratic institutions, while Kabila's renamed Democratic Republic of Congo shows the need for leaders to establish democratic rule to help forestall civil wars.
"These issues and all the other difficult problems will be looked at during the summit," said Ibrahim Dagash, spokesman for the OAU secretariat.
"The African leaders will not dodge any issues," he told reporters on the eve of the June 2-4 OAU summit where over 30 heads of state and government, including Kabila, are expected.

But diplomatic sources told Reuters that a two-day OAU foreign ministers' conference that ended on Friday had hardly debated "the hard facts" of former Zaire or of Sierra Leone, where junior army officers staged a coup a week ago against President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah who was democratically elected a year ago.
The foreign ministers had instead made strenuous efforts to avoid discord, they charged.

"It's not the sort of debate people were expecting on these issues. The first session was very formal, repeating condemnations in the case of the Sierra Leone coup and repeating congratulations in the case of the new Democratic Republic of Congo," said a Zimbabwean diplomat who declined to be identified.

Real debate on the former Zaire must involve discussing fears, privately expressed by some African leaders, that Kabila's victory could be the start of a new chapter in Africa with some countries openly backing the overthrow of neighbouring governments, the diplomats said.

Although they have denied it, Rwanda, Burundi, Uganda and Angola are among states that Mobutu's 32-year-old regime -- regarded as one of the world's most corrupt dictatorships -- accused of militarily backing Kabila's whirlwind rebel campaign.

The foreign ministers reiterated the OAU's condemnation of the Sierra Leone coup and said the 53-member organisation was looking to the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) to help restore constitutional rule.
Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge denied suggestions that Nigeria, which is leading the ECOWAS programme, had the OAU's blessing to use military force against the coup leaders.
"We never discussed the mechanics," he said last Thursday.

Such a discussion, some delegates say, would plunge the OAU into a debate on the morality of ECOWAS, which is dominated by military-led Nigeria, in leading others towards democracy. ECOWAS members Ghana and Burkina Faso are also led by ex-coup leaders.

The OAU encourages members to participate in peacekeeping and political mediation programmes around the continent, but has been wary of blessing anything that might be seen as outright political interference which is outlawed by its charter.
OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim says the OAU summit will also discuss the peace processes in Angola, Somalia and Liberia.
"But we want this summit to focus on economic development," he said, adding that emphasis would be placed on how Africa can realise its quest for an economic community by 2030.
